# Part 2 — Step 3, fully dissected

## Overview: what this step is actually for

Steps 1–2 answered *"what exists"* (outcomes, requirements). Step 3 answers a completely different question: ***"what caused what."*** This is the step that operationalizes the paper's core idea — **Desideratum 2: Direct and Indirect Influence** — the distinction between an action that *explicitly* creates a requirement versus an action that *quietly seeds* one that forms later. This is the mechanism your whole thesis is built on.

**Cadence:** once **per requirement** — an even finer fan-out than Step 2. If outcome 6 has 3 requirements, that's 3 separate Step 3 calls, each examining one requirement's full web of influence.

## The four inputs, one by one

**`{outcome description}`** — **ECHO**, straight from Step 1b. Gives the model the bigger context this requirement sits inside.

**`{req id}` / `{req text}`** — **ECHO**, straight from Step 2's output for this one requirement.

**`{req origin turn}`** — this one is **DERIVED, not given directly.** Step 2's output doesn't have a field called "origin turn" — it has `creation_action_ids` (a list, potentially several ids, as we saw with outcome 6/req1's `["U(1,6)", "U(1,7)"]`). The origin turn is *computed*: take the earliest of those ids. This matters because everything else in this prompt is defined relative to that boundary.

**Section A / Section B — the most important design decision in this whole step, and it's a real asymmetry:**
- **Section A (Preceding) = the WHOLE dialogue so far, not just this outcome.** I confirmed this from the paper's own text: *"we compute cosine similarity between tr and **all preceding turns**"* — no outcome restriction. This is deliberate — it's the only mechanism that can catch **indirect influence across outcomes** (a seed planted while discussing something else entirely, three outcomes ago).
- **Section B (Subsequent) = same outcome only.** The prompt says this explicitly: *"within the same outcome."* This makes sense — fulfilling a requirement logically happens in its own thread, not somewhere unrelated.

**One rule that's not written in the prompt text but is forced by the paper's math (§B.1.1, Eq. 1):** *"Actions in the origin turn receive maximal direct influence (Idir=5.0)."* This means the `creation_action_ids` themselves must be **excluded** from both candidate sections — they don't get judged by the LLM at all, they get an automatic fixed score. Judging them would be circular (asking "is this connected to itself").

## The five relationship types — and a real asymmetry worth understanding

| Type | Definition | Natural home |
|---|---|---|
| **DIRECT CONNECTION** | Explicitly *operates on* the requirement — creates/revises/tightens/deletes/requests/evaluates/fulfills it; the requirement is the *object* of the action | Rare in Section A (nothing before creation can "revise" something that doesn't exist yet, except the edge case of a near-duplicate earlier request); more natural in Section B |
| **IMPLICIT CONNECTION** | Provides *context* that motivates/triggers the requirement, without being directly about it | **This is the indirect-influence concept — the whole point of the step.** Most natural in Section A (the seed, planted earlier) |
| **IMPLEMENTS** | *(Section B only, explicitly restricted in the prompt)* — directly executes/fulfills the requirement | The natural Section-B label for "AI did the work this required" |
| **CONTRIBUTES** | Partial work/context/progress toward the requirement, weaker than IMPLEMENTS | Section B's equivalent of IMPLICIT — supportive but not fulfilling |
| **NO CONNECTION** | Default | *"Default to NO CONNECTION unless clear semantic evidence"* — the prompt is explicitly conservative |

## The score — this is literally the paper's math, not a separate metric

`relationship_score` **is** the value `I(a → r)` from Equation 1 (`I = I_dir + I_ind`). 1–3 for IMPLICIT/CONTRIBUTES, 4–5 for DIRECT/IMPLEMENTS, null for NO_CONNECTION. This single field, once produced, feeds directly into `M(p,r) = Σ I(a→r)` (Eq. 2) — the speaker-level total. **Nature:** the *band* (1-3 vs 4-5) is CLASSIFIED (determined by which type you picked), but the *exact number within the band* is a graded judgment call — closer to SYNTHESIZED.

## Two real problems I found, worth knowing before you run this

**Problem 1 — a genuine schema mismatch inside the prompt itself.** The TASK section calls the field `"explanation type"` and lists 6 named categories, implying you pick one. But the OUTPUT schema literally only shows `"explanation": "..."` — a single free-text field, no separate enum. **This is ambiguous as written.** The cleanest resolution: treat the 6 names as a *controlled vocabulary prefix*, writing the value as `"Option-Select: user picked the classroom-locations idea directly from the option AI listed earlier"` — one field, category + justification combined. **[OURS — resolving an inconsistency the prompt itself doesn't resolve.]**

**Problem 2 — this is the bigger finding.** I checked the paper's own published research (§3.2, Table 2 and Table 6, Appendix D) for its real influence-pattern taxonomy, and it's **not the same 6 categories this prompt uses.** The paper's actual, published taxonomy has **11 named subtypes in 4 categories:**

| Category | Subtypes |
|---|---|
| **Underspecified Intent/Preference** | State Broad Goal→Derive Concrete Req · Implicit Preferences→Explicate Into Reqs |
| **Artifact-Triggered Elaboration** | Deliver Artifact→Add Refinement Req · Provide Context→Build Req Around It · Lay Out Plan→Form Procedural Req |
| **Problem-Triggered Revision** | Expose/Report Problem→Add Corrective Req · Reveal Complexity→Add Simplification Req |
| **Interactional Steering** | Present Options→Select/Specify Choice · Ask for Recommendation→Devise Strategy · Invite Extension→Specify Next Steps · Request Implementation→Include Setup |

The prompt's 6 names (Feedback-Adopt, Option-Select, Preference-Accumulate, Failure-Triggered-Requirement-Add, Preference-Realize, Intent-Reveal) only loosely map onto some of these 11 — e.g. `Option-Select` ≈ "Present Options→Select/Specify Choice." **Why the mismatch exists:** a footnote in the paper reveals the 11-pattern taxonomy came from *"one author qualitatively summariz[ing] 11 patterns from a sample... up to 20 pairs [per category] were reviewed"* — a **separate, manual, small-sample research analysis done after the fact**, not the operational vocabulary fed to the automated Stage-3 LLM at scale. So: **the 6-category prompt is what actually runs at scale; the 11-pattern taxonomy is the authors' own later manual research finding.** They're not meant to be identical — different purposes, different stages. Worth deciding whether you want to extend Step 3's vocabulary to the fuller, more precise 11 (better research grounding) or keep the simpler 6 (matches the actual automated prompt as designed).

This asks the model to re-state SHAPER/EXECUTOR/OTHER for an action **that already has a `role` field from Step 1a.** Checking the paper's own math: `M(p, ρ, r) = Σ 1[role(a)=ρ] I(a→r)` (Eq. 3) uses `role(a)` as a **fixed property of the action**, decided once, in Stage 1 — not re-derived per-requirement. So `contribution_role` here should, in principle, **always match** what Step 1a already assigned that action. Two honest readings: either it's a **consistency check** (compare against Step 1a's role, flag any mismatch as a possible extraction error) or it's genuinely redundant. I'd treat it as the former — free error-detection, not wasted effort.

**One precise mathematical detail worth knowing:** the paper's own K definition is `K = {SHAPER, EXECUTOR}` — **explicitly excluding OTHER.** This means an action tagged `role=OTHER` in Step 1a can still contribute to the *unsplit* total `M(p,r)`, but can **never** appear in the *role-split* `M(p,ρ,r)` — meaning it would be invisible to a SHAPER-vs-EXECUTOR breakdown (like your eventual DIRECTION bar), even if it has real influence. | Field | Nature | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `index` | **ECHO** | Just repeats the number you assigned when assembling the input — not the model's judgment |
| `action id` | **ECHO** | Same — copies which action this label is about |
| `relationship type` | **CLASSIFIED** | One of the 5 types |

| `explanation` | **SYNTHESIZED** | Should combine category + justification per Problem 1's resolution |
| `contribution role` | **CLASSIFIED** | Should match Step 1a's `role` for this action — treat mismatches as a red flag |

## What the passage actually says, in plain terms

Study [58] watched humans and AIs create together in networks and noticed something: when the AI's ideas didn't match a person's vision, **nobody argued.** There was no explicit "no, I want it this way" moment. Instead, people quietly **absorbed AI concepts into what they still experienced as "their own original work."** The dispute was settled invisibly, inside the person's head — by *assimilation* (taking the AI's idea in) or *compromise* (meeting it halfway). The paper calls this **implicit negotiation**: a negotiation that happens without anyone noticing it's happening.

And then the twist: these hybrid networks produced the **greatest creative diversity** — without any formal negotiation interface. Study [59] agrees: disputes get settled by *complementary cooperation* (AI brings scale and pattern synthesis, humans bring context, intentionality, moral judgment), not by overt bargaining.

## The headline connection: this is your thesis in a different vocabulary

Read that first sentence again next to your own project: *"people integrate AI-generated concepts into their own original work"* — without noticing. That is, almost word for word, the blind spot your entire project exists to expose: **AI-authored specificity that users accept without realizing it.** What the paradoxes paper calls *implicit negotiation*, COTRACE calls *indirect influence*, and your panel calls *"X of your choices were the AI's idea."* Three vocabularies, one phenomenon. Your lightbulb metric is, quite literally, an **assimilation counter** — the first instrument I'm aware of in either paper's frame that makes implicit negotiation *measurable* rather than just observable in a lab study.

This is why the passage upgrades my earlier verdict. I told you Individual vs. Collective was the one paradox your system doesn't touch — and for the *style-homogenization* face of it, that's still true (you don't analyze aesthetics). But the paradox has a second face the paper poses as an open research question: *"How do designers and AIs settle creative disputes and which interface features work best for negotiating a common course?"* Your pipeline is a settlement-recording instrument. That's a real claim on this paradox — I was wrong to score it zero.

## The deeper mappings, concretely

**Your open-slot lifecycle is a dispute-settlement ledger.** Look at what a slot actually is through this passage's lens: an *open, unsettled point of negotiation* between individual vision and collective suggestion. The `resolve` op records the settlement — *who* settled it and *how*. And your resolution data can be read in exactly the paper's settlement vocabulary: a resolve where the user's firm answer adopts the AI's hedge = **assimilation**; a revise that modifies an AI-seeded requirement = **compromise**; a user override with their own idea = **assertion**. `Abandon` = a dispute that dissolved unsettled. You could even add this as a classification on resolve ops — a settlement-type field — and it would be directly grounded in this passage.

**Step 3's explanation vocabulary is a taxonomy of negotiation moves.** "Feedback-Adopt" *is* assimilation, by name. "Option-Select" is a settled negotiation over AI-offered alternatives. The paper asks *which interface features work best for negotiating* — your pipeline already labels the moves by which negotiations conclude. You can answer their open question with data.

The 3D chat's P2 (AI authoring the architecture through your underspecification) is an **assimilation-settlement**. You have real settlement data on disk right now.

## Is showing this a good thing? The honest two-sided answer

**The case for yes is in the paper's own next paragraph.** Right after your quoted passage, it warns of the echo-chamber risk and states the design objective: *"creating interfaces that empower users to **consciously modulate** their interaction with the collective knowledge base."* Conscious modulation logically **presupposes visibility** — you cannot consciously modulate an influence you cannot perceive. Your tool is the perception layer that "consciously" requires. That's a direct textual hook, not an inference.

**But the caution is in your quoted passage itself, and take it seriously:** the hybrid networks achieved their greatest diversity *without* formal negotiation interfaces — implicit, frictionless assimilation apparently *works*. Which means: assimilation is not a failure state. If your panel frames "8 of your choices were the AI's idea" as an accusation, it misrepresents what the evidence says is a healthy synergy mechanism — and risks two bad outcomes: users defensively rejecting AI ideas just to look agentic (gaming the metric), or feeling shamed for collaboration functioning as collaboration should. **The design consequence: the settlement record must be neutral — a ledger, not a verdict.** "This idea originated with the AI and you adopted it" is information; "the AI is driving you" is a judgment the evidence doesn't license.

**And one genuine vindication:** this passage partially defends your ambient, non-interrupting design — the thing I critiqued as "passive" two turns ago. For *this* paradox specifically, the evidence says formal negotiation interfaces aren't needed and heavy interruption might disrupt the very flow that produces synergy. A retrospective mirror that doesn't interpose itself in the negotiation, but makes the settlement legible afterward, is arguably the *correct* touch-weight here — active friction remains the right prescription for Speed/Reflection and Control/Serendipity, but not necessarily for this one. The paradoxes want *different* intervention weights, which is itself a design insight worth writing down.

Strong claims: **Speed vs. Reflection, Originality vs. Remix, Ambiguity vs. Precision** (open slots). Partial: **Control vs. Serendipity** (detection without veto). **R0 (root = chat title): good, and defensible on paper grounds.** The vision stays in the *user's own words* — the individual's framing anchors the whole structure, which is exactly the "human provides vision, intentionality" role the paper's [59] citation assigns. No change needed.

## How the YouTube philosophy actually translated

Not the aesthetic — the *principle*: in a comment thread, **the line is the relationship.** One continuous thin rail connects parent to replies, so you trace lineage by following it, never by decoding indentation. Your current tree uses fragmented elbow glyphs — each one a disconnected hint. So the structural redesign (landing at V1) is: **one continuous rail from root to the deepest visible node, with the root→current segment lit** in a soft blue. That lit path is the signature element of the section — it answers "where am I, inside what?" purely by eye. The second borrowed move is that collapse markers ("⋯ 2 more", "⋯ collapse dropped") sit **on the rail itself** as chips, exactly like "94 replies ∨" sits on the thread line — the rail is where hidden things announce themselves.

## The key decisions per stage, and why

**V1 (origin tint):** the crucial choice is that it introduces **zero new vocabulary** — blue/orange is the encoding DIRECTION already teaches two inches below. Two deliberate exemptions: the **root stays neutral** (it's the chat's identity, not a contribution to score), and **only the dot is tinted, never the text** — provenance marker, not judgment, which is the ledger-not-verdict principle from the negotiation discussion made into a pixel rule. One real consequence surfaced by designing this: your rulebook now **needs a split-dot rule** — "One Less" was co-created (creation actions from both speakers), which neither pure blue nor pure orange can honestly render. The half-and-half dot is that rule; it wasn't needed until origin became visible.

**V2 (slot badges):** the metaphor is **dashed = not yet solid** — dashed badge, dashed expansion border, and (in the state variant) a dashed hollow dot. One metaphor doing all the ambiguity work, no new colors. The expanded rows carry origin mini-dots — *who raised the hedge* — which quietly brings the implicit-negotiation data into the goal panel. And I folded the **exploring state** in here as a variant card, because it's the same philosophy: the panel claims focus only when focus exists. You're right, and the diagnosis is worth stating plainly: I designed that board for *us* — the people who built the pipeline and are proud of the data — not for the person glancing at a sidebar mid-work. Orientation is this section's whole job. Everything I layered on was detail, and detail belongs behind a tap, later, if ever. Let me rebuild from your one-sentence definition and nothing else.

Rebuilt from your one-sentence definition only: *what am I doing now, and a small hint of what came before.*

## The whole design

Two elements. A small grey **breadcrumb** — `start › … › previous` — and one bold **focus line** with a single tiny label: `NOW`. That's it. The pattern is a breadcrumb, which every user already knows from folders and websites — zero concepts to learn, nothing to decode. You were right about the labels too: MAIN GOAL and CURRENT SUB-GOAL are gone. Size and position do that work — small grey above, big bold below reads as "context / current" without a word of vocabulary.

The file shows the same design across all four scenarios that exist: chat just started (no breadcrumb at all — empty context is shown by absence, not an empty label), one level in, deep in (the middle collapses silently into `…` — the vastness stays in the data, never on the screen), and the honest state when nothing is settled ("Exploring — nothing settled yet", written as a plain sentence a stranger understands, not a symbol they'd have to learn).

## The constraints that keep it from ever growing back

This is the part that answers your "put constraints so it doesn't become complicated" — six hard rules in the file, the important ones being: **three rows max, forever**, regardless of how big the real tree gets; **one bold thing** — if two elements compete for the eye, the design has failed; **one word of label**; and **nothing else in the resting view, ever** — no dots, badges, chips, or markers.

Everything from before — origin, open questions, dropped paths — isn't deleted, just demoted: candidate tap-to-reveal details, considered one at a time, later, and each one only survives if the resting view still passes the test that now governs this section: **a stranger glances for three seconds and can say "they're working on X, inside Y."** That's the acceptance criterion for any future addition, and it's the constraint that keeps the pipeline's richness underneath the surface instead of on it.

Let me check the paper directly to see where this prompt actually sits in their architecture — whether it's part of the core attribution pipeline or something else — before judging its relevance to your design.

Confirmed from the source — and the placement matters a lot here. This prompt (plus a companion right after it that you'll want too) is **not part of the core attribution pipeline at all**. Let me lay out the full analysis, then update the document.

## What this actually is, and where it sits in the paper

This is the first half of a two-prompt **evaluation suite** the paper uses in §4.2 — not a "Step 4." The pair is:

1. **Deliverable Extraction** (what you pasted) — per outcome, scan the dialogue and pull out the final concrete artifact verbatim (code, plan, itinerary...), or report none exists.
2. **Requirement–Deliverable Evaluation** (the very next prompt on the same page) — take that deliverable text + the outcome's requirements, and check each requirement: reflected in the artifact, true/false, with evidence.

Together they compute one number: **Requirement Satisfaction Rate** — what fraction of the requirements actually got met in the final output. The paper built this to answer its §4.2 question ("does more goal-shaping improve output quality?" — answer: basically no, Pearson ≈ −0.002). Two honesty flags straight from the source: **the validation table (Table 4) covers only Goal/Requirement/Influence accuracy — these two prompts have no reported validation at all**, and the input `{dialogue turns}` ("RELEVANT DIALOGUE TURNS") is **never defined anywhere** — the same category of under-specification as `dialogue_summary` was.

## Is this important for your design? Yes — but not where the rest of the pipeline lives

Everything you've built so far answers *who shaped the goals*. This layer answers a question your panel currently can't: ***were the goals actually met?*** Three specific reasons it earns a place:

**1. It closes the loop.** Your rail shows 13 requirements extracted, influence traced, DIRECTION bar computed — but nothing anywhere verifies fulfillment. "You two set 13 requirements; the final artifact satisfies 9" is a genuinely different kind of information than anything the panel currently displays.

**2. The paper's own finding here is directly your thesis.** §4.2's sharpest result: **35.3% of assistant-created requirements are fully implemented in the same turn they're introduced** — the AI writes the test and immediately passes it, with the user never touching that loop at all. That's the purest form of the invisible micro-decision your whole project is about. A "self-served requirements" count (AI-created + AI-fulfilled, zero user involvement) is computable from data you already have (Step 3's IMPLEMENTS labels + creation turns) once this layer exists.

**3. It gives your open slots a third, genuinely new detection point.** Here's the extension worth adding: a slot that's still *open* in conversation can be **silently resolved inside the artifact** — the deliverable just *commits* to one option (a tool, a structure, a style) even though nobody ever decided it out loud. That's an invisible decision *materialized* — arguably the most on-thesis signal in the entire system, and neither the paper's version nor anything we've built so far catches it. I've added an optional slot-check section to E2 for exactly this.

## Where it does NOT belong: the live per-pair loop

This is the important architectural judgment. Unlike Steps 1a–3, this layer should **not** run per pair — a deliverable usually doesn't exist until late, re-extracting it every pair is waste, and the verbatim-extraction requirement makes it the most token-heavy prompt in the system (it must return to the **raw transcript** — the first prompt since 1a to do so, because actions are paraphrases and can't reconstruct verbatim artifact text). Right cadence: **session-end or on-demand** ("check goal satisfaction now"). Which means its natural home in your design is the **report/summary layer — your Screen-Time analogue** — and notably, *satisfaction rate is a serious candidate for that report's headline metric*, one of the three intake decisions you left open earlier.

Now updating the document — new section, renumbering, both prompts clean with changes tables:

One stale reference caught by verification (the regex treated "§8." at end-of-sentence as a subsection prefix) — fixing:

Document updated to v4 — new §8 (Evaluation Layer), everything renumbered cleanly, all 13 code blocks verified free of inline annotations.

## Summary of the analysis and what went into the doc

**What it is:** not "Step 4" — it's the paper's two-prompt **evaluation suite** (the one you pasted, plus its companion **Requirement–Deliverable Evaluation** on the same page, which is useless without and pointless before the first one). Together they compute Requirement Satisfaction Rate. I named them **E1/E2** in the doc specifically to avoid colliding with the paper's actual Stage 4 (Quantification, the math layer).

**Should it be in your design — yes, with a firm placement decision:** it belongs in the **report/session-summary layer, never the live per-pair loop.** Documented cadence: session-end or on-demand. Three reasons it earns the spot: it closes the loop the panel currently leaves open (goals *set* vs. goals *met*); the paper's 35.3% same-turn self-satisfaction finding maps to a computable **"self-served requirements"** metric (AI wrote the success condition AND fulfilled it, user touched neither); and — the addition I'd argue is the most on-thesis thing in this whole layer — the **open-slot silent-resolution check** I added to E2: the artifact quietly commits to one answer for a question nobody ever decided in conversation. That's an invisible micro-decision *materialized*, and neither the paper nor anything we'd built before catches it. All three derived metrics (satisfaction rate, self-served count, silent resolutions) are specified in §8.2.5 as code-computed, not model-reported.

**Changes made to the paper's prompts** (all in legend tables, prompts clean): turn ids switched from bare integers to a new **turn-level** format `U(x)`/`A(x)` — deliberately coarser than action-level `U(x,y)`, because a deliverable lives in a whole turn, not one atomic action; and E1's `{dialogue turns}` input **defined** — the paper never defines "RELEVANT DIALOGUE TURNS" anywhere, the same under-specification class as `dialogue_summary` was. Our rule: raw text of every turn containing ≥1 action bound to the outcome.

**Honesty entries added (§11.8):** no published validation exists for either prompt (Table 4 covers only Goal/Req/Influence); our `{dialogue turns}` rule is our own unvalidated definition; E1 is the most token-expensive call in the system; and `is_reflected` is deliberately coarse binary — treat satisfaction numbers as indicative, not precise.

One connection worth holding onto: **satisfaction rate is a strong candidate for the headline metric of your Screen-Time report idea** — one of the three intake decisions you left open there. This layer is essentially that report's data source arriving for free.

## 4. HOW section — the paper's idea in the simplest possible terms

The BCG paper's core observation, stripped of all jargon: **when people work with AI, the collaboration itself has a shape, and there are three recognizable shapes.**

You divide the work: you decide *what* and *why*, you hand the AI a bounded task, it executes, you take the output back. The seam is visible — anyone watching can say "that part was the human's job, that part was the machine's." In your driving metaphor: **you're driving; the AI is the navigator you consult.**
- **Cyborg** — no seam. The work is interwoven at a fine grain: you write half a thought, the AI completes it, you redirect, it reshapes — neither party's contribution is separable from the other's. Machine and human fused rather than stacked. Driving metaphor: **you're both steering — hands overlapping on the wheel.**
- **Self-automator** — the third mode (and the one the BCG authors flag as the risk case): the human delegates not just execution but *the deciding itself*. The AI proposes what to do AND does it; the human's role shrinks to pressing accept. The seam is gone in the other direction — the human is barely in the loop. Driving metaphor: **autopilot — you're in the seat, but the car is driving.**

The crucial philosophical point the paper makes — and why this section must stay non-preachy: **none of these is inherently wrong.** Centaur is great for tasks you understand; Cyborg is where genuinely new ideas happen; even Self-automator is fine for stakes-free chores. Which means the section's entire job is to make the mode *visible*, never to grade it. A user who sees "autopilot" on a grocery-list chat should feel zero shame; a user who sees "autopilot" on their thesis chapter should feel a flicker of "wait, is that what I want?" — and that flicker coming from *them*, not from us, is the whole design.

## 1. Goal section — corrected

You're right, and the horizontal breadcrumb was my drift, not your design. Restored to your prototype's structure: **vertical, indented branches, reading down like a tree collapsing toward the present.** Content rule: always exactly three nodes — **main goal → the goal just above the latest → the latest goal.** And all labels gone — no "MAIN GOAL," no "CURRENT SUB-GOAL," no "NOW," no "exploring." ## 2. Timeline — the overall goal, properly stated this time

You're right that I defined elements without defining the section. Here it is:

**The timeline is the chat's factual record — the answer to "what actually happened here, and who made it happen?"** The goal section shows intention; the timeline shows *events*. Its collapsed state gives a scannable rhythm of the whole conversation — one line per exchange, each showing what occurred and who drove it — so a person can read the *shape* of a session in five seconds. Its expanded state is the receipt behind any one exchange: the actual decisions (requirements) that were born or changed there, and which side shaped them. Its deepest level (level 2) is the proof: the exact text, the extraction, the influence trail with evidence. **Three depths, one principle: every level down answers "show me" about the level above.** Scan → record → proof.

## 3 & 4. Collapsed row and drawer — simplified as instructed

Collapsed row is now three things: **pair label · turn-delta bar · summary line** (+ the expand chevron). LIVE pill and viewing bar deleted — correct call, your prototype already carries that state in the panel's top status ("VIEWING P2 · HISTORY / LIVE"), so repeating it per-row was redundant encoding.

Drawer is now exactly two kinds of content: **the requirements of that turn** — each as `R-label + spine bar showing which side it leans` — **and that turn's open slots**, shown plainly. Forward thread, recovery flag, mini legend: all cut. The labeling system: chat-wide running numbers in creation order (R1, R2, R3…), revisions get a suffix (R2a) — your trace's own convention, which gives you the reviewable, referenceable system you asked for.

And the deeper layer is now formally **a second expansion level**: tap a requirement inside the drawer → it opens to show its exact text, how it was extracted, and the direct/indirect influence detail with evidence quotes — the place where the pipeline's full output finally surfaces. Its internal design is deferred (as you said), but its *existence and job* is now in the spec, so the drawer above it can stay minimal without losing anything.

## 5. Your cumulative-vs-per-turn question — this one needs your confirmation

The honest answer: both are defensible, and I previously specced it as cumulative, but **your instinct is better, and here's the reasoning.** If the drawer bar shows *cumulative* mass, then R2's bar in P5's drawer includes shaping that happened in P2, P3, P4 — the drawer stops being a record of *this turn* and starts repeating history that other turns already told. That's redundant data, which you've consistently cut. If the bar shows **only the mass added this turn**, then each drawer is a self-contained record of exactly what happened there — and stacking all drawers genuinely reconstructs the whole story with no double-counting. The requirement's *full* cumulative story still exists — it just lives one level down, in the level-2 expansion, where you look when you care about one requirement's whole life.

So the proposed rule: **drawer bars = this turn's added mass only; cumulative per-requirement bars = level-2.** Confirm this and it locks.

## 6. HOW section — the paper's plain meaning, then real metaphors people already know

The paper's own meanings, stripped bare: **Centaur** = division of labor with a visible seam — the human decides, hands over a bounded task, takes the result back. **Cyborg** = no seam — contributions interleaved so tightly neither party's work is separable. **Self-automator** = the human hands over the *deciding itself*, not just the doing — and the paper's warning is only about doing this unknowingly.

You're right that "driving" strains — it's good for two modes but has no natural Cyborg. Candidate metaphor families, judged on one criterion — does a normal person get it *instantly*:

**Kitchen family (my recommendation):** Centaur = *you're the chef, the AI is your kitchen hand* — you decide the dish, it chops. Cyborg = *cooking together* — both hands in the same pot, tasting and adjusting each other's moves. Self-automator = **you ordered delivery** — food shows up, you didn't cook. That last one is the blatant, universally-known image you asked for: everyone instantly understands the difference between cooking and ordering in, and it carries exactly the right connotation — totally fine sometimes, but if you *only* ever order delivery, you know what happens to your cooking. The skill-atrophy implication is *built into the metaphor itself*, without the panel saying a preachy word.

**Music family (runner-up):** you sing lead, AI plays backup / jamming together / **lip-syncing** — the AI plays while you mime. Lip-syncing is vivid and slightly funnier, but it carries a whiff of accusation (faking it) that violates your non-judgment rule. **Journey family (weakest):** driver+GPS / co-pilots / passenger — passenger is decent but Cyborg has no honest car image; this is exactly where the current design strains.

My call: kitchen. But this is a taste decision that's genuinely yours — pick the family and I lock it into the spec with the three fixed sentences.

## Idea 2: the Influence Ledger — the one [OURS] piece of architecture

The paper adds its numbers once, over a finished chat. Your panel needs the same numbers *at every pair*, scrubbing backward. The mechanism: every score, the moment it's born, becomes one row — `(pair_added, action_id, speaker, role, outcome, req, score, kind)` — in an **append-only ledger**. The subtle field is `pair_added`: it's the pair whose pipeline pass *produced* the score, not the pair the action happened in — that's what makes Trigger-B incremental labels land in the right time bucket. Then every single panel number is a *query* over this table: the Direction bar is a running sum, the turn-delta is one pair's rows, the Decisions counter is a group-by over creation rows, drawer bars are per-requirement filters.   relationship_score, kind = "labeled".
- Any requirement that arose via a resolve op: its KNOWN SLOT ORIGIN labels =

- NO CONNECTION labels: no row.
- Open (unresolved) and abandoned slots: no rows.

M(AI, r)  = sum of scores with speaker A
M(you, SHAPER, r), M(you, EXECUTOR, r), M(AI, SHAPER, r), M(AI, EXECUTOR, r)
(role-split sums; rows with role OTHER count in M(p,r) but in NO role-split sum)

PART 3 — PAIR TOTALS AND DIRECTION
Δ(1, you) = sum of ALL ledger scores with speaker U
Δ(1, AI)  = sum of ALL ledger scores with speaker A
C(1, you) = Δ(1, you); C(1, AI) = Δ(1, AI)   (first pair, so cumulative = delta)
Direction: you% = C(1,you) / (C(1,you)+C(1,AI)) × 100, AI% = remainder.

AI-count  = # requirements with creator A

The HOW section exists almost entirely for this. The underlying problem: in a long AI chat, "who's actually doing this work" becomes genuinely fuzzy in your head after enough turns — you *feel* like you're steering, but you can't say precisely when that stopped being true. The mechanism: the two-question structure from the source study (**Q1: who selected what needs doing, Q2: who identified how**) turns a vague feeling into a computed, per-turn fact — Centaur, Copilot, or Autopilot, stated in a metaphor everyone already understands. ## Authorship — directly and mechanically solved, more than any other item on your list

This is the Decisions counter, the Direction bar, and the SHAPER/EXECUTOR role tags working together. The core move: every requirement traces to a *creator* (earliest creation action, U or A prefix) — so "whose idea was this" stops being a memory or a feeling and becomes a stored fact with a verbatim quote behind it. The evidence chain (quote → action → requirement → score → ledger row → pixel) is precisely built so authorship claims are never "I think it was mine" but "here's the sentence." This is the one place the design achieves something close to *proof*, not just impression.

## Agency of choice — the deepest one, and the one closest to your actual thesis

This is subtler than authorship. Authorship asks "whose idea was it"; agency of choice asks "did I know a choice was being made at all." The mechanism built specifically for this is the **open-slot lifecycle**: when something hedged or uncertain comes up ("maybe X, we'll decide later"), it doesn't get silently swallowed into a firm requirement, and it doesn't get silently dropped either — it's tracked as an open question, with an explicit `origin` (did *you* raise the uncertainty, or did the AI). That's the mechanism that catches the choice point *before* it disappears. And the mode line's honest neutrality is what protects the rest: if the system just labeled things "good/bad," you'd stop noticing your own choices and start reacting to the system's judgment instead — agency would just shift target. Stating "Autopilot" with the same visual calm as "Driving" is what keeps the noticing act yours.

## Control conflict — solves a real but narrower thing than the label implies

Worth being precise here: this isn't conflict between two people negotiating — it's *silent transfer of control within one collaboration*, which is a different (and arguably harder) problem, because there's no second party to notice and object. What actually catches it: the E2 slot-check extension I flagged earlier — checking whether a final artifact **silently resolved an open question that was never decided in conversation**. That's the purest form of "control was ceded and nobody said so." The design's answer isn't prevention (the panel doesn't stop you from delegating) — it's *detection*, surfaced without accusation, so an unnoticed handoff has a chance to become a noticed one.

## Cognitive overload — the one with a genuine internal tension, worth being honest about

Here's the uncomfortable truth: a panel showing five kinds of information is a **candidate cause** of cognitive overload, not just a cure for it. The earlier design-critique round caught exactly this (too many simultaneous encodings, unlabeled symbols). What the design does — the three-second glance test, the fixed-size goal section, one bold current line, R-DISPLAY collapse, "no textual state labels anywhere" — isn't eliminating overload in general; it's specifically fighting the overload *the panel itself would otherwise cause*, while addressing a different, real overload: the cost of **mentally reconstructing "what happened and who did it"** across a long session without any external record. Before this panel, that reconstruction lived entirely in your head; now it's offloaded to something you can glance at or dig into on demand. So the honest claim is narrower than "solves cognitive overload" — it's "moves the burden of tracking provenance out of your head, while working hard not to create a new burden in its place." Whether that trade succeeds is genuinely still being tested (it's exactly why the legend/onboarding item is still flagged open).

**The one thread connecting all five:** every mechanism above does the same underlying thing — it takes something that would otherwise stay *implicit* (a role, an authorship claim, a choice point, a ceded decision, a mental reconstruction) and makes it a *stored, traceable fact*. **Role ambiguity** means: in a given moment of a collaboration, it's unclear — even to the person themselves — who is actually playing which role. Concretely, two roles are getting confused:

- **Who's deciding** *what* needs to happen (the direction-setter)
- **Who's doing** the actual work to make it happen (the executor)

In a normal AI chat, these blur together fast. You ask a question, the AI answers with an opinion baked into the answer, you say "yeah sure," and three exchanges later you genuinely can't say whether *you* decided the approach or the AI did and you just went along with it. Nobody announced a role — it just drifted. That's the ambiguity: not conflict, not a fight over control, just **fog about who was actually holding which job at any given point.**

Concrete example from your own design's language: at pair 5, was the user "driving" (they decided the goal, AI just executed) or was the AI "flying" (AI proposed the direction *and* built it, user just said "ok")? Both can *feel* similar in the moment — a smooth, cooperative exchange — but they are structurally opposite in terms of who held the "what" role versus who held the "how" role. Role ambiguity is that structural difference being invisible to the person living through it.

**Why it's a real problem, not a nitpick:** if you can't tell which role you were in, you can't accurately judge your own skill development, you can't tell a colleague "I built this" versus "I directed this" honestly, and — the thing your thesis cares about most — you can't notice the moment your role quietly shifted from decider to approver. That's the exact mechanism of the skill-atrophy-without-noticing problem: the role changed, but no signal marked the change, so you kept thinking of yourself as "doing the work" long after you'd stopped.

**How your HOW section resolves it, specifically:** it takes that fog and turns it into a computed, stated fact — Centaur (you held both roles), Copilot (roles shared/interleaved), Autopilot (AI held both roles) — per turn, with a running distribution. The ambiguity doesn't go away because the collaboration becomes simpler; it goes away because the *role itself gets named out loud*, turn by turn, instead of staying an unexamined feeling.

## The correction that matters most

**What you designed is technically a popover, not a tooltip** — and this isn't pedantry, it's a naming fix that changes which component the builder reaches for. The standard distinction: a *tooltip* is hover-triggered, plain text, no close button, vanishes when you look away. A *popover* is click-triggered, holds richer content, and needs its own explicit dismissal — exactly what you spec'd (click the i, panel opens, dismiss via X or tap-outside). Telling Figma Make "popover" instead of "tooltip" gets you the right accessibility behavior automatically, since the two patterns are governed by different rules.

Checked against Nielsen Norman Group's own test for when on-demand disclosure (vs. permanent on-screen text) is appropriate: *"is the information necessary to complete a task? If no, this pattern is well suited."* Our popups pass cleanly — the panel is fully usable without ever opening one; they exist purely for orientation. And the "same pattern, 5 times, no exceptions" rule you already had turns out to be a documented principle too: NN/g flags inconsistent treatment as a real failure — if only some icons explain themselves, people stop trusting the ones that don't.

Pricing checked and current. Here's the honest recommendation for *your* workload specifically, then setup.

## The recommendation: one provider, two models — and it's already what your Phase 2 brief configured

Current Anthropic API pricing: Haiku 4.5 at $1/$5 per million tokens (input/output), Sonnet 4.6 at $3/$15, Opus-class at $5/$25. Your engine has two very different kinds of jobs, and they map cleanly onto the two cheap tiers:

**MODEL_FAST = `claude-haiku-4-5`** → Steps 1a and 1c. These are exactly what Haiku is built and priced for — high-volume extraction and classification. Splitting turns into atomic actions doesn't need deep judgment; it needs speed, structure-following, and low cost.

**MODEL_MAIN = `claude-sonnet-4-6`** → Steps 1b, 2, 3, and the live chat replies in Phase 3. These are the judgment steps — the requirement gates, the hedge/slot decisions, the influence scoring — where a cheap model making sloppy calls would poison your ledger, which is the one thing in this system that must be right. Sonnet 4.6 is the price/quality sweet spot for production work, and using it for the chat too means **one provider, one API key, one SDK** — the "easy" you asked for.

Why not something cheaper still? Ultra-budget models (GPT-nano-class, DeepSeek) exist at a fraction of Haiku's cost — but only for the classification-type work, adding a second provider, second key, and second failure mode to save cents on the *least* important steps. Not worth it at your scale. And don't use Opus/Fable in the *engine* — that tier is for Claude Code writing the engine, not for the engine's own calls; Sonnet-class is fully sufficient for the pipeline's judgment.

## What it will actually cost you (rough, honest math)

Your heaviest known case — the Style-DNA pair 1 (42 AI actions, 14 requirements, big Section-A labeling) — pencils out to roughly **$0.40–0.70 for the whole pair** on this split. Typical later pairs (1–3 requirements touched) more like **$0.10–0.20**. A full 8-pair Budget-chat engine run: **$1–2**. All of Phase 2's development and testing, including re-runs and mistakes: realistically **$5–15 total**. New API accounts typically include about $5 in free credit at signup, which alone nearly covers initial development. This is genuinely a cheap project — the per-pair loop is small; there's no scale multiplier until you have users.

One future lever worth knowing but *not* building yet: **prompt caching (90% off cached input)** — your pipeline's growing `{all actions block}` is the textbook use case for it. That's a Phase 5 optimization; note it, skip it now.

## Setup — five minutes, four steps

1. **console.anthropic.com** → sign up (this is separate from any Claude.ai subscription — Pro/Max don't include API access).
2. Billing → add **$5–10 prepaid credit** (pay-as-you-go, no subscription; set auto-reload *off* so a bug can't silently spend). Optionally set a monthly spend limit as a tripwire.
3. **API Keys → Create Key** → copy it once (it's shown once).
4. In your repo: `cp .env.example .env`, then set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...` — done. Your Phase 2 brief already specifies `engine/config.py` reading `MODEL_FAST` (default `claude-haiku-4-5`) and `MODEL_MAIN` (default `claude-sonnet-4-6`) from env, so **no code or brief changes are needed** — the defaults are exactly this recommendation.

One small caution flag for the build: the correct Haiku model string in the API is the dated ID (`claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` per the docs; `claude-sonnet-4-6` works undated) — if the engine ever throws a model-not-found, that's the first thing to check, and it's a config value, not a code fix.

## The real comparison (current verified prices, per 1M tokens in/out)

| Provider | Fast tier (Steps 1a/1c) | Main tier (1b/2/3 + chat) | Your heavy pair ≈ | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Three honest observations that matter more than the raw prices:

**The prompt–model fit argument favors OpenAI more than I credited.** The authors' own repository defaults to GPT — meaning the pipeline's prompts (which we copied near-verbatim) were developed and validated against GPT-family behavior. That's a real, non-price reason.

**Gemini's free tier is the standout for your situation.** Development is where you'll burn tokens on mistakes and re-runs — and Gemini's API free tier (rate-limited, but fine for a sequential per-pair pipeline) can carry all of Phase 2 at literally $0. You also already have a Google account wired up via Antigravity.

**DeepSeek's caveat is worth saying plainly:** it's absurdly cheap and quality is credible, but data goes to servers in China — for a thesis artifact built by a student in Germany, that's a GDPR/optics question you don't need, and practitioner reports flag reliability wobbles. Fine as an experiment, not as the foundation.

## Revised recommendation

**Primary: Google Gemini** — `MODEL_FAST = gemini-3-flash`, `MODEL_MAIN = gemini-3.1-pro` (or Flash for everything first, upgrading Steps 2/3 to Pro only if label quality disappoints). Free tier through development; pennies after. **Runner-up: OpenAI mini/nano tiering** — nearly as cheap, plus the prompt-fit argument. **Keep Anthropic as the quality fallback** for Step 3 specifically if either's labeling proves sloppy — that's the one step where paying 3× can be worth it.

## The one architecture change this requires — and it's small and strictly good

Build `engine/llm.py` against the **OpenAI SDK with a configurable `base_url`** instead of the Anthropic SDK. Gemini, DeepSeek, and OpenAI all expose OpenAI-compatible endpoints — so one code path gives you **all three providers as pure config**, switchable per-step, no code changes. (The official repo made the same move — it's multi-provider via a gateway.) Give this amendment to your Phase 2 session, replacing the brief's S1 LLM-layer paragraph:

```
AMENDMENT to PHASE2_BRIEF S1 (from command center): engine/llm.py is built on the
OpenAI SDK with env-configurable base_url — NOT the Anthropic SDK. Env vars:
LLM_BASE_URL, LLM_API_KEY, MODEL_FAST, MODEL_MAIN (defaults: Gemini's
OpenAI-compatible endpoint, gemini-3-flash / gemini-3.1-pro). Everything else in S1
unchanged: retries, llm_monitor.txt full logging, json repair, frozen prompts.
Update .env.example accordingly.
```

## Setup (Gemini path — the cheapest start, ~3 minutes)

1. **aistudio.google.com** → sign in → **Get API key** → create key (free tier active immediately, no card needed).
2. In `.env`: `LLM_API_KEY=<your key>` and `LLM_BASE_URL=https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/openai/`.
3. That's it for Phase 2. If you later hit free-tier rate limits mid-run, either let the engine's retry/backoff ride it out (sequential pipeline = it just goes slower), or enable billing — at ~$0.10–0.40 per heavy pair, a full Budget-chat run is still under a dollar.

One quality gate to keep yourself honest: when Phase 2's S8(c) comparison report lands, eyeball the Step-3 labels specifically — if Gemini's scoring looks noticeably sloppier than your manual Sonnet-era runs, that's the moment to flip `MODEL_MAIN` to Sonnet 4.6 for Steps 2/3 only and eat the small cost difference. The env-var architecture makes that a 10-second change.

## Two facts to get straight first

**Your Google AI Pro plan does not include Gemini API usage.** The subscription covers the Gemini app, NotebookLM, Flow credits — and, usefully for you, it *does* provide the fixed developer quota when you sign into **Antigravity / Gemini CLI with your Google account** (AI Pro is an officially supported tier there). **Correcting myself:** as of April 2026, **Pro-series models left the API free tier** — Gemini 3.1 Pro is paid-only via API now. So my earlier "3.1 Pro for free" was stale. The good news: the free tier still covers the Flash class, and that currently includes **Gemini 3.5 Flash** — Google's newest fast model, genuinely strong — plus 3.1 Flash-Lite. For your pipeline, Flash-class free is a real plan, not a compromise: sequential per-pair calls with exponential backoff ride the free tier's rate limits fine (429s just make it slower, never wrong).

One honesty flag you should weigh: **on the free tier, Google may use your prompts/outputs to improve its models.** Your engine will be processing your own chats — thesis data. If that bothers you, the paid tier (still pennies) doesn't train on your data. Your call; just making it visible.

## Setup — step by step (~5 minutes)

1. Go to **aistudio.google.com**, sign in (same Google account as your AI Pro is fine — keeps everything in one place, though it doesn't affect API billing).
2. Left sidebar → **"Get API key"** → **Create API key** (it creates a Google Cloud project behind the scenes; no credit card needed for free tier).
3. **Check your live limits** at AI Studio's rate-limit page for your project — the docs are explicit that limits are per-project and shown live there, so trust that page over any table you read online (including mine).
4. In your repo's `.env`:

LLM_BASE_URL=https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/openai/
MODEL_FAST=gemini-3.1-flash-lite

MODEL_FAST / MODEL_MAIN          → the two tiers
MODEL_STEP2 / MODEL_STEP3        → optional per-step overrides (fall back to MODEL_MAIN)
